newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania president meets opponents as truce expires.
newsitem.headline: Albania president meets opponents as truce expires.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha and his opponents were deadlocked on Sunday in attempts to end an armed rebellion in the south as insurgents consolidated their hold on major towns.
A ceasefire ordered by Berisha in the army's drive against the insurgents in exchange for an amnesty expired early on Sunday, with no word on whether it would be extended.

Nor was there was any indication that government troops were preparing to move against the rebels, now well armed after breaking into army munitions depots. Rebels have rejected the amnesty and demand Berisha's resignation.

Opposition politicians said Berisha met members of his own Democratic Party and 10 other groupings for eight hours, long into Saturday night, pressed by two European mediation missions seeking an end to violence.
The talks were likely to be resumed on Sunday.
The politicians said the discussions had reached broad agreement on holding fresh elections within two to three months.
But they ran into trouble over Berisha's insistence that he would not allow the Socialists, heirs to Albania's communist party, into an interim government.

"We need a government made up of all parties which will win the confidence of those people now in rebellion," Socialist Party leader Rexhep Mejdani told Reuters on Sunday. "But Berisha said there was no place in any government for the Socialists."

In the south, rebels organised themselves into defence councils to guard against any new assault by government troops under emergency rule introduced by parliament after the latest violence erupted a week ago. At least 20 people have died.

A journalist reached by telephone in the Adriatic port of Vlore said demonstrators were out in force -- as they have been since protests began last month against the collapse of shady investment schemes with the savings of hundreds of thousands.
Sporadic shooting was less widespread than in recent days and the local defence council was in session.
Gjirokaster, the last government-held town in the south fell to the rebels on Saturday, when government troop reinforcements were sent scurrying in disarray.
The insurgents ransacked a barracks and town residents helped themselves to food from shops and government depots.

The talks in Tirana followed two European mediation missions this week aimed at halting the violence and finding a political compromise after last May's general elections criticised as unfair by the opposition and Western observers.

Former Austrian leader Franz Vranitzky met Berisha twice on Saturday and said the Albanian leader was considering an extension to the ceasefire and had shown flexibility on new elections. A European Union delegation held similar talks last week.

But in an interview printed in the Democratic Party daily Rilindja Demokratike, the only daily appearing under emergency regulations, Berisha's top adviser Genc Pollo dismissed any cooperation with the Socialists.
"I personally consider it quite dangerous to accept in government a political party which leads an armed revolution," Pollo said. "This offers it a chance to clean its hands."
Socialist leader Fatos Nano is in jail after being convicted of corruption. The opposition says he is a political prisoner.
Some opposition politicians suggested that Berisha was giving some ground in response to outside mediation efforts.
"I am more optimistic after (Saturday's) talks," Paskal Milo of the Social Democratic party told Reuters. "Berisha is in a desperate situation. He has very little room for manoeuvre."
